sourceApproval: Founder-approved under DEC-040 (adapted to Physics Academy rigor)
prerequisites: Lessons 1–8 of this unit — signed position and displacement, position-time and velocity-time and acceleration-time graphs, the constant-acceleration equations, free fall, and vector components.
majorObjective: Integrate the whole unit: move fluently among a verbal description, position-time, velocity-time, and acceleration-time graphs, and the constant-acceleration equations for one motion; run the vector decomposition round trip; and judge whether an unfamiliar real-world claim about motion is actually supported by the information given.
subObjectives: Given any one representation of a constant-acceleration motion, produce the other three consistently.
Use slope and area to connect the three motion graphs (slope of $x$-$t$ is $v$-$t$; slope of $v$-$t$ is $a$-$t$; area runs the other way).
Decompose a vector into components and rebuild its magnitude and quadrant-correct direction.
Decide what a stated claim about motion does and does not establish, and name the missing information when a claim is underspecified.

hook.prompt: An object's velocity-time graph is a straight line rising from zero. What do its position-time and acceleration-time graphs look like?
choices: Position-time: upward curve that steepens. Acceleration-time: horizontal line above the axis.
Position-time: straight rising line. Acceleration-time: straight rising line.
Position-time: horizontal line. Acceleration-time: upward curve.
Both are straight lines through the origin.

priorKnowledge: This lesson introduces no new physics. It practises connecting everything from Lessons 1–8 on single problems, the way the unit test and later units will demand.

chunks.title: One motion, four representations
chunks.concept:
A single constant-acceleration motion can be told four ways — in **words**, as a **position-time** graph, as a **velocity-time** graph, and as an **acceleration-time** graph — plus the **equations**. They must all agree.

The graphs are linked by slope and area:

- Slope of the **position-time** graph at a time = the **velocity** at that time.
- Slope of the **velocity-time** graph = the **acceleration**.
- Area under the **acceleration-time** graph = the **change in velocity**; area under the **velocity-time** graph = the **displacement**.

So if you are given any one representation, you can build the others: differentiate (read slopes) to go “down” the chain $x \to v \to a$, or accumulate (read areas) to go “up” it.
chunks.representation:
To convert between representations:

1. Identify what you are given (words, or which graph).
2. To get the next graph down ($x \to v$, or $v \to a$): read the slope of each segment.
3. To get the next graph up ($a \to v$, or $v \to x$): read the signed area, and remember the starting value ($v_i$ or $x_i$).
4. Check the verbal description against every graph: sign, constancy, pattern of change.

conceptFigures.caption: One motion — starting from rest with constant positive acceleration — shown three ways. The position-time curve steepens; the velocity-time line rises straight; the acceleration-time line is flat.

workedExample.problem: An object starts at rest at the origin. Its velocity-time graph is a straight line from $(0\ \mathrm{s},\ 0)$ to $(4\ \mathrm{s},\ +12\ \mathrm{m/s})$. Describe the acceleration-time graph and the position-time graph, and find the displacement over the $4\ \mathrm{s}$.

phases.label: Acceleration-time graph (slope of v-t)
steps: The velocity-time graph is one straight line, slope $= (12 - 0)/(4 - 0) = +3\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
So the acceleration-time graph is a horizontal line at $+3\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ for the whole interval.

phases.label: Position-time graph (area of v-t, and shape)
steps: The velocity grows steadily from $0$, so the position-time graph starts flat (velocity $0$) and gets steeper — an upward-curving line from the origin.
Its steepness at each time equals the velocity at that time.

phases.label: Displacement (area under v-t)
steps: Area under the velocity-time line is a triangle: $\Delta x = \tfrac{1}{2}(4\ \mathrm{s})(12\ \mathrm{m/s}) = +24\ \mathrm{m}$.
Check with an equation: $\Delta x = v_i t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(3)(4)^2 = +24\ \mathrm{m}$. Agrees.

workedExample.keyMove: Slope takes you $x \to v \to a$; area takes you $a \to v \to x$. The equations are a shortcut for the same relationships.

formativeCheck.question: An object's position-time graph is a straight line with a constant positive slope. What do its velocity-time and acceleration-time graphs look like?
choices: Velocity-time: horizontal line above the axis. Acceleration-time: horizontal line on the axis.
Velocity-time: rising straight line. Acceleration-time: horizontal line above the axis.
Velocity-time: horizontal line on the axis. Acceleration-time: horizontal line on the axis.
Velocity-time: upward curve. Acceleration-time: rising straight line.

feedback.correct: Correct — a constant slope on the position-time graph means constant velocity: a horizontal velocity-time line above the axis. Constant velocity means zero acceleration: a horizontal acceleration-time line on the axis.

incorrect.1: A rising velocity-time line would come from a position-time graph that curves (steepening), not a straight one.
incorrect.2: A velocity-time line on the axis is zero velocity — but the position is changing (positive slope), so the velocity is a non-zero constant.
incorrect.3: Curves and rising lines correspond to changing velocity. A straight position-time graph has constant velocity.

hint: Slope of position-time = velocity. A constant slope means what kind of velocity? Then slope of that velocity graph = acceleration.
formativeCheck.solution: A straight position-time graph has one constant slope, so the velocity is a non-zero constant: the velocity-time graph is a horizontal line above the axis. A constant velocity has zero slope, so the acceleration-time graph is a horizontal line sitting on the axis ($a = 0$).

chunks.title: The vector round trip
chunks.concept:
When motion or a quantity has a direction that is not simply $+$ or $-$ along one line, use the **vector round trip** from Lesson 8:

- **Magnitude + angle → components:** the component along the reference axis uses cosine, the perpendicular one uses sine (re-derive from the triangle; watch which axis the angle is measured from). Attach signs from the direction.
- **Components → magnitude + direction:** $V = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$ (positive); quadrant from the signs of $v_x$ and $v_y$; reference angle from $\tan^{-1}(|v_y|/|v_x|)$.

The two directions are consistent only if a decomposition and a reconstruction of the same vector give back the same magnitude and direction.
chunks.representation:
For a vector problem inside a motion question:

1. Draw the vector and its right triangle; mark the reference angle and the axis it is measured from.
2. Go the direction the problem needs (components, or magnitude + direction).
3. Verify by going back the other way and checking you recover the start.

workedExample.problem: A drone's displacement is $50\ \mathrm{m}$ at $37^\circ$ north of east. Take east as $+x$, north as $+y$; use $\sin 37^\circ = 0.60$, $\cos 37^\circ = 0.80$. Find the components, then reconstruct the magnitude and direction to check.

phases.label: Components
steps: Angle measured from east ($+x$). East component is adjacent: $v_x = 50\cos 37^\circ = 50(0.80) = +40\ \mathrm{m}$.

phases.label: Reconstruct the direction
steps: Both components positive → first quadrant (north-east). Reference angle $= \tan^{-1}(30/40) = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 37^\circ$ above east — matches the given direction.

workedExample.keyMove: Decompose, then reconstruct: if the magnitude and direction come back unchanged, the work is consistent.

formativeCheck.question: A boat's velocity has components $v_x = -12\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (east positive) and $v_y = +5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (north positive). What is its speed, and roughly which way is it heading?
choices: Speed $13\ \mathrm{m/s}$; heading north-west (up and to the left).
Speed $17\ \mathrm{m/s}$; heading north-east.
Speed $7\ \mathrm{m/s}$; heading south-west.
Speed $13\ \mathrm{m/s}$; heading north-east.

incorrect.1: $17\ \mathrm{m/s}$ adds the component magnitudes ($12 + 5$). Speed is $\sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$. And $v_x$ is negative, so it is not heading east.
incorrect.2: $7\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is $12 - 5$, which is not the rule. And $v_y > 0$ means north, not south.
incorrect.3: The magnitude is right, but $v_x$ is negative (west) and $v_y$ is positive (north), so the heading is north-*west*, not north-east.

hint: Speed $= \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$. Direction: $v_x$ negative means west; $v_y$ positive means north.
formativeCheck.solution: Speed $= \sqrt{(-12)^2 + (5)^2} = \sqrt{144 + 25} = \sqrt{169} = 13\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The signs $v_x < 0$, $v_y > 0$ place the velocity in the second quadrant — west and north — so the boat heads north-west.

chunks.title: Transfer: what does a claim actually establish?
chunks.concept:
An unfamiliar real-world claim about motion often states **less than it seems to**. The transfer skill is to separate what the claim **does** establish from what it **does not**, and — if it is underspecified — to name the missing piece.

Common gaps:

- A **speed** or speedometer reading fixes speed but not direction (so not velocity, and not whether velocity is constant).
- A **displacement** fixes the net change but not the path or the distance.
- A **final position** relative to a start tells you the sign of the displacement but nothing about speeding up or slowing down.
- A **single acceleration value** does not tell you whether the object speeds up or slows down — you also need the sign of the velocity.
chunks.representation:
For any claim about a motion:

1. Restate exactly what quantity is given (speed? displacement? position? acceleration?).
2. List what that quantity does fix.
3. List what the claim asserts beyond that — and mark each as supported or not.
4. If not supported, name the specific extra information that would settle it.

workedExample.problem: A news report says: “The drone travelled 2 km in 5 minutes, so it must have been flying at a constant speed of 24 km/h.” Evaluate the claim.

phases.label: What is actually given
steps: A distance (or displacement) of $2\ \mathrm{km}$ over a time of $5\ \mathrm{min}$.

phases.label: What that fixes
steps: The **average** speed: $2\ \mathrm{km} / 5\ \mathrm{min} = 0.4\ \mathrm{km/min} = 24\ \mathrm{km/h}$. That part of the arithmetic is fine.

phases.label: What the claim asserts beyond that
steps: “Constant speed” — not supported. The drone could have flown fast, hovered, and sped up again, with the same average.
It also says nothing about direction, so “constant velocity” is even less supported.

phases.label: Name the missing information
steps: To claim constant speed you would need the speed at several instants (or a statement that it was held steady) — and to claim constant velocity, also that the direction never changed.

workedExample.keyMove: “Distance over time” gives an average, never a guarantee that the motion was steady.

formativeCheck.question: A coach says: “The sprinter's displacement was $100\ \mathrm{m}$ down the track and her acceleration was negative the whole race, so she must have finished slower than she started.” Which response is correct?
choices: The claim is fully supported — negative acceleration always means finishing slower.
The claim is not reliably supported — whether she finished slower depends on the sign of her velocity relative to her acceleration, not on the acceleration's sign alone.
The claim is wrong because displacement cannot be $100\ \mathrm{m}$ if she is slowing.
The claim needs the exact acceleration value to evaluate.

feedback.correct: Correct — a negative acceleration slows an object only while its velocity is positive. If “down the track” is the negative direction, a negative acceleration would speed her up. The acceleration's sign alone does not settle it.

incorrect.0: Negative acceleration means “finishing slower” only when the velocity is positive. Compare the signs.
incorrect.2: Displacement and speeding up/slowing down are unrelated. She can cover $100\ \mathrm{m}$ whether her speed rises or falls.
incorrect.3: The exact value is not the issue — even with a number, you would still need the sign of her velocity to decide.

hint: Does a negative acceleration always slow an object down? What else do you need to know?
formativeCheck.solution: Whether an object speeds up or slows down depends on the sign of its acceleration *compared with* the sign of its velocity — same sign speeds up, opposite signs slow down. The coach gives only the acceleration's sign. If “down the track” were the negative direction, a negative acceleration would actually speed her up. The claim is underspecified; you need the direction (sign) of her velocity.

misconceptions.question: A position-time graph and a velocity-time graph are shown side by side for the same motion. At $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$ the position-time graph is at its highest point (a smooth peak). What is true of the velocity-time graph at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$?
choices: It is also at its highest point.
It crosses zero — the slope of the position-time graph is zero at a smooth peak, and that slope is the velocity.
It is at its lowest point.
Nothing can be said without numbers.

feedback.correct: Correct — at a smooth peak the position-time graph is momentarily flat, so its slope (the velocity) is zero. The velocity-time graph passes through zero at that instant.

incorrect.0: The height of the position-time graph and the height of the velocity-time graph are different quantities. A peak in position means zero *slope*, not a peak in velocity.
incorrect.2: The velocity is zero at the peak, not at a minimum. Whether the velocity-time graph is rising or falling there depends on the acceleration.
incorrect.3: The key fact needs no numbers: a smooth maximum has zero slope, and slope of position-time is velocity.

hint: The velocity is the *slope* of the position-time graph. What is the slope at the top of a smooth hill?
misconceptions.solution: At a smooth maximum, the position-time graph is instantaneously horizontal, so its slope is zero. Since the slope of the position-time graph is the velocity, the velocity is zero at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$ — the velocity-time graph crosses the time axis there. This is the height-versus-slope distinction applied across two graphs at once.

errorAnalysis.studentWork:
Problem: An object's velocity-time graph is a horizontal line at $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ from $0$ to $6\ \mathrm{s}$. Sketch its position-time and acceleration-time graphs (it starts at $x = +10\ \mathrm{m}$).

Student's response: “The velocity is negative and constant. Position-time graph: a horizontal line at $-4$, because the velocity is $-4$. Acceleration-time graph: a horizontal line at $-4$, same as the velocity.”
prompts: State what the slope of a position-time graph represents, and what the slope of a velocity-time graph represents.
Identify both errors in the student's sketches.
Give the correct position-time and acceleration-time graphs, with values.
errorAnalysis.modelResponse: The slope of a position-time graph is the velocity; the slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration. Error 1: the student drew the position-time graph as a horizontal line at $-4$ — but a constant velocity of $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ means the position *changes* at a steady rate, so the position-time graph is a straight line with slope $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$, starting at $x = +10\ \mathrm{m}$ and falling to $x = +10 + (-4)(6) = -14\ \mathrm{m}$ at $t = 6\ \mathrm{s}$. Error 2: the acceleration-time graph is not “same as the velocity.” The velocity-time graph is horizontal, so its slope — the acceleration — is zero: the acceleration-time graph is a horizontal line on the time axis ($a = 0$).

representationConnections: Every representation in this unit is one of: words, a position-time graph, a velocity-time graph, an acceleration-time graph, an equation, or a vector (magnitude + angle, or components). Slope moves down the graph chain ($x \to v \to a$); area moves up it ($a \to v \to x$); the equations shortcut the same links; SOHCAHTOA and the Pythagorean theorem convert between a vector and its components. A correct solution has all of them agreeing.

lessonAssessment.question: An acceleration-time graph is a horizontal line at $-2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ for $5\ \mathrm{s}$. The object starts with $v_i = +6\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Which description of its velocity-time and position-time graphs is correct?
choices: Velocity-time: straight line from $+6$ falling to $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Position-time: rises, levels off at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$, then falls.
Velocity-time: horizontal at $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Position-time: straight falling line.
Velocity-time: straight line from $+6$ rising. Position-time: upward curve.
Velocity-time: falls to zero at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$ and stays there. Position-time: rises then flat.

feedback.correct: Correct — constant $a = -2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ gives a velocity-time line of slope $-2$: from $+6$ down to $+6 + (-2)(5) = -4\ \mathrm{m/s}$, crossing zero at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$. The position rises while $v > 0$, peaks at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$, then falls.

incorrect.1: A horizontal velocity-time graph would need zero acceleration. Here $a = -2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, so the velocity changes steadily.
incorrect.2: Negative acceleration means the velocity-time line *falls*, not rises.
incorrect.3: The velocity does not stop at zero — the acceleration keeps acting, so it continues to $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The position does not go flat; it starts decreasing after the peak.

hint: Constant negative acceleration → velocity-time line with a constant negative slope. Where does it cross zero? The position peaks there.
lessonAssessment.solution: The acceleration is a constant $-2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, so the velocity-time graph is a straight line of slope $-2$: it runs from $v_i = +6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ down to $v = +6 + (-2)(5) = -4\ \mathrm{m/s}$, crossing zero at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$. The position-time graph rises (positive velocity) until $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$, reaches a smooth peak there (velocity zero), then falls (negative velocity).

lessonAssessment.question: “Car A and car B both travel from town X to town Y — the same $60\ \mathrm{km}$ — in exactly $45\ \mathrm{minutes}$.” Which conclusion is guaranteed?
choices: They had the same average velocity for the trip.
They had the same speed at every instant.
They took the same route.
Neither ever stopped.

feedback.correct: Correct — average velocity is total displacement over total time. Same start and end points (same displacement) and same time means the same average velocity, regardless of what happened in between.

incorrect.1: Equal averages do not force equal instantaneous speeds — one car could have sped and slowed differently and still matched the average.
incorrect.2: Displacement depends only on the endpoints. The cars could have taken different roads of different lengths.
incorrect.3: Either car could have stopped and made up time elsewhere without changing the trip's total time.

hint: Average velocity = (displacement) / (time). Which of those two is the same for both cars?
lessonAssessment.solution: Both cars have the same displacement (X to Y) and the same total time, so their average velocities are equal — that is guaranteed. Nothing else is: instantaneous speeds, routes, distances travelled, and whether they stopped are all unconstrained by the information given.

lessonAssessment.scenario:
Take east as positive. A cart's motion over $10\ \mathrm{s}$ is given by a velocity-time graph of three straight segments:

| Segment | Interval | Velocity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $0$ s to $4$ s | constant $+3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |
| 2 | $4$ s to $6$ s | straight line from $+3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $-3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |
| 3 | $6$ s to $10$ s | constant $-3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |

The cart starts at position $x_i = 0$.

parts.prompt: (a) Find the acceleration on each segment.
parts.modelResponse: Segment 1: horizontal, $a_1 = 0$. Segment 2: $a_2 = \Delta v / \Delta t = (-3 - 3)/(6 - 4) = -6/2 = -3\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Segment 3: horizontal, $a_3 = 0$.

parts.prompt: (b) Find the displacement during each segment (use areas; segment 2 crosses zero at $t = 5\ \mathrm{s}$).
parts.modelResponse: Segment 1: $(+3)(4) = +12\ \mathrm{m}$. Segment 2: above the axis from $t = 4$ to $5\ \mathrm{s}$, triangle $\tfrac12(1)(3) = +1.5\ \mathrm{m}$; below from $t = 5$ to $6\ \mathrm{s}$, triangle $\tfrac12(1)(3) = -1.5\ \mathrm{m}$; segment 2 total $= 0\ \mathrm{m}$. Segment 3: $(-3)(4) = -12\ \mathrm{m}$.

parts.prompt: (c) Find the cart's final position at $t = 10\ \mathrm{s}$, and sketch (in words) the shape of its position-time graph.
parts.modelResponse: Final position: $x = x_i + (+12) + 0 + (-12) = 0\ \mathrm{m}$ — back at the start. Position-time graph: a straight rising line (slope $+3$) from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, +12)$; then a smooth curve rising to a peak of about $+13.5\ \mathrm{m}$ at $t = 5\ \mathrm{s}$ and curving back down to $+12\ \mathrm{m}$ at $t = 6\ \mathrm{s}$; then a straight falling line (slope $-3$) back to $(10, 0)$.

examConnection: The unit test and later units expect you to switch representations without being told which one to use, and to spot when a stated claim outruns its evidence. This lesson is the rehearsal: one problem, all the tools.
summary: One constant-acceleration motion has four consistent representations — words, position-time, velocity-time, acceleration-time — plus the equations. Slope moves down the chain ($x \to v \to a$); signed area moves up it ($a \to v \to x$). Vectors convert to components with SOHCAHTOA and back with the Pythagorean theorem plus a quadrant check. For an unfamiliar claim, separate what is given (speed? displacement? position? acceleration?) from what the claim asserts, and name the missing information when the claim is underspecified.

exitQuestion.question: For a certain motion, the acceleration-time graph is a single horizontal line above the time axis. Which pair of graph shapes must the velocity-time and position-time graphs have?
choices: Velocity-time: straight line with constant positive slope. Position-time: upward curve that steepens.
Velocity-time: horizontal line. Position-time: straight line.
Velocity-time: upward curve. Position-time: straight line.
Velocity-time: horizontal line above the axis. Position-time: upward curve.

feedback.correct: Correct — a constant positive acceleration is a positive slope on the velocity-time graph (a straight rising line), and a steadily rising velocity makes the position-time graph curve upward with increasing steepness.

incorrect.1: A horizontal velocity-time line means zero acceleration. Here the acceleration is a positive constant, not zero.
incorrect.2: The velocity-time graph is a straight line (constant slope = constant acceleration), not a curve. The curve appears one level up, in position-time.
incorrect.3: A horizontal velocity-time line is constant velocity, i.e. zero acceleration — contradicting the given positive acceleration.

hint: Constant acceleration → constant slope on the velocity-time graph. A steadily increasing velocity → what shape of position-time graph?
exitQuestion.solution: A constant positive acceleration means the velocity-time graph has a constant positive slope — a straight rising line. The velocity therefore increases steadily, so the position-time graph gets steeper and steeper over time: an upward-curving line (the shape of $x = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ from rest).
